title: The Cost of Consistency
author: Such, Christopher
summary: Christopher Such uses his own uneven journey through phonics and maths teaching to examine the real tradeoff schools make when they require consistent programmes and approaches across all staff. He argues that prescriptive, checked schemes genuinely help less experienced or less expert teachers reach adequacy, but they also frustrate the school's most expert teachers, whose hard-won judgment gets constrained by a script built for the average case. Such traces his own shift in view: as a classroom teacher he resented losing autonomy to a prescriptive maths scheme, but once he took responsibility for quality across a whole school, "universal adequacy" became his first priority even at the cost of frustrating his strongest teachers. He is careful not to claim the compromise is avoidable, listing the genuine collective benefits of consistency (mutual support, targeted CPD, familiar routines for pupils) while also naming what gets lost, including the possibility that expert teachers only fully develop through being left to find their own way. The piece closes by calling for more honest conversations within schools about which costs of consistency are worth paying, rather than pretending the tradeoff doesn't exist.
points: Such's core argument is that consistency and teacher autonomy are in real tension, not a false dichotomy resolved by "support the weak, free the strong" — school leaders usually cannot reliably identify who is genuinely expert.

He names a specific mechanism for the cost of prescriptive schemes: expert teachers who feel "boxed in" quietly disengage or grow frustrated, and that frustration often surfaces as pushback against curriculum resources or programmes generally.

He flags his own change in perspective once he moved from classroom teacher to whole-school leader, using it as evidence that the "cost of consistency" argument looks different depending on the leader's vantage point.
Such explicitly extends the argument beyond phonics to maths schemes, behaviour management, and ECF mentoring, framing it as a sector-wide tension rather than a subject-specific one.
quotes: But sensible doesn’t mean flawless. It’s easy to tell staff that a new scheme or a new structure will provide benefits for all, but often this just isn’t true.

But I felt different once I was required to take on some responsibility for the quality of teaching across an entire school. Suddenly, my first priority was universal adequacy, even where that placed constraints on the most expert teachers in the school.

There are also subtle gains from consistency that compound: teachers can better support each other, professional development can be better targeted and interventions can build more readily on routines that are familiar to all pupils.

I suspect that the pushback against systematic phonics teaching and detailed curriculum resources, for example, is frequently the conduit through which stifled voices within the profession try to make themselves heard.

We need honest conversations about the compromises that are deemed necessary, ones that will allow us to include on the balance sheet all of those often-hidden items like the demotivation of more experienced colleagues and the potential loss to the profession of their expert presence in the classroom.
